tagline: Limestone bluffs and river towns link two great river confluences.
intro: The Meeting of the Great Rivers Scenic Route follows 33 miles of southwestern Illinois river country, with bends along forested bluffs and towns beside the water. Part of the Great River Road, it is also a National Scenic Byway. The Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau emphasizes its scenery, archaeology and history; the Illinois tourism office highlights the roadway between limestone bluffs and the Mississippi.

At Elsah, the opening of the Great River Road in 1964 marked a change for a village that had remained quiet after its shipping trade declined. The scenic route received Illinois designation in 1998. National designation followed in 2000, when the corridor was extended from East Alton south to New Poag Road.

Traveling from the northern end, begin at Pere Marquette State Park and follow the route through Grafton, Elsah and Alton. A parallel bike trail accompanies the road between the park and Alton, with the Confluence Bike Trail continuing toward Hartford. At Alton, the corridor includes the Clark Bridge and the National Great Rivers Museum at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam. The southern end reaches the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site near the meeting of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers.

moments.title: Pere Marquette State Park
moments.text: Pere Marquette’s lodge is a piece of the park’s early history, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s. The park began in 1931 as Piasa Bluffs State Park and soon took its present name. The lodge was expanded in 1985; a visitor center followed in 1997 with exhibits on local history and ecology. The Illinois River borders the park on the west and south. In late winter, hundreds of bald eagles congregate in and near the park to catch fish, arriving from wetland nesting areas to the north.

moments.title: Grafton
moments.text: Limestone from Grafton’s quarries became part of bridges and public buildings beyond the town’s riverfront. Quarries supplied stone for the Eads Bridge in St. Louis and the Jersey County Courthouse, while boatbuilding and commercial fishing supplied other work. The Old Boatworks south of Main Street included a paint house and machine shop where paddle wheelers and later PT boats were built. The historic district connects Main Street to the river by way of Maple Street and the wharf. Built of limestone in 1846, that wharf replaced an earthen landing lost to a flood.

moments.title: Elsah
moments.text: Elsah’s stone houses began with an offer: James Semple, who founded the village in 1853, gave free lots to people who built with stone from his quarry. The village became a shipping point for Jersey County farm produce, then lost importance as the railroad arrived. Its entire village entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. LaSalle Street’s commercial district extends three blocks inland from the river and consists mainly of stone buildings. On Mill Street, residential sections include stone and brick houses and a block of Greek Revival homes.
moments.notice: LaSalle Street’s historic commercial district is built mainly of stone.
